title: MG Marg rules: Gangtok's car-free street, fines and manners
meta_description: MG Marg in Gangtok is car-free, smoke-free, spit-free and litter-free. What the rules are, what fines have been set, plastic rules and street manners.
summary: MG Marg is Gangtok's main street, a car-free stretch of about 1 km in the town centre. Smoking, spitting and littering are banned, and Gangtok's municipal fines have been ₹200 for smoking or spitting and ₹200–5,000 for littering. Keep to the benches, bins and footpath manners and you will have no trouble.

sections.heading: What MG Marg is and why it has rules
paras: Mahatma Gandhi Marg, which everyone calls MG Marg, is the heart of Gangtok. It runs for about 1 km through the town centre, lined with shops, cafes, bakeries, hotels and travel desks, with a row of benches and planters down the middle and a statue of Gandhi about halfway along. No vehicles of any kind are allowed on it, and the state promotes it as a spit-free, litter-free and smoke-free zone. Boards at the entrances say so.

The rules are not decoration. Sikkim has built its tourism around being clean, and Gangtok's residents take that personally. A visitor who drops a wrapper on MG Marg is likely to be told about it by a shopkeeper before any official arrives. Most visitors find this the most pleasant evening street in the eastern Himalaya precisely because of the rules, so we brief every guest before their first walk.

sections.heading: The rules, one by one
paras: These are the rules as we understand them in 2026. Enforcement is real, especially in peak season, and it applies to tourists exactly as it applies to locals.
list: No vehicles. Cars, taxis, two-wheelers and cycles are not allowed on the street. Drivers drop you at either end.
No smoking. Smoking in public places is banned across India under the 2003 tobacco law, and Gangtok enforces it on MG Marg.
No spitting, including paan and gutka. This is the rule visitors from the plains most often break without thinking.
No littering. Use the bins; if you cannot find one, carry the rubbish back to your hotel.
No plastic carry bags. Shops pack goods in paper or cloth; carry your own bag.
No polystyrene (thermocol) plates or cups, which Sikkim has banned statewide.
Do not sit on the planters or climb the statues for photos.
Keep music and voices down, especially after 9 pm when hotels on the street want quiet.

sections.heading: Fines you could face
paras: Gangtok Municipal Corporation set out its penalty levels in a 2018 presentation on cleanliness, and these are the figures most often quoted. Amounts and enforcement change, so check current status before you travel. In practice, most first-time offenders get a warning and a stern word; repeat offenders and anyone arguing get the fine.
Smoking in public is also covered by India's national tobacco law, which allows a fine of up to ₹200. Police and municipal staff patrol MG Marg in the evening, especially in peak season.

If you are stopped, stay calm and polite. A genuine official will be in uniform or carry an ID card, will tell you which rule you broke, and will give you a receipt for any fine paid. Pay only against a receipt, and do not hand cash to anyone who cannot show identification. If you think the fine is wrong, note the official's name and ask your hotel to help you raise it the next morning rather than arguing on the street.

sections.heading: Plastic, bottles and what to carry
paras: Sikkim has been tightening plastic rules for years. The state has banned polystyrene products and has barred packaged plastic water bottles from government functions and meetings, and shops in Gangtok are licensed on the condition that they do not hand out banned plastic. You will see cloth and paper bags everywhere and few plastic bottles on the street.

For visitors this means three small habits. Carry a cloth or folding bag for shopping on MG Marg and Lal Bazaar. Carry a refillable water bottle; most hotels and many cafes will refill it with filtered water. And keep a small pouch for your own wrappers, tissues and bus tickets, because bins on MG Marg can be full on busy evenings.
If you smoke, use the designated spots away from the street that your hotel will point out, and carry a pocket ashtray. Cigarette ends are the litter that annoys residents most.

Shopping on MG Marg is mostly fixed-price, and that is part of the street's appeal. Look for Sikkimese tea from Temi, the state's tea estate in the south, packets of large cardamom (Sikkim grows more of it than any other Indian state), hand-woven bags and Tibetan-style carpets from the craft shops. Keep the receipts; they help if anything needs exchanging before you leave town.

sections.heading: Street manners locals notice
paras: Beyond the written rules, a few unwritten ones will make you welcome.

Families with small children and older travellers find MG Marg one of the easiest streets in the hills: it is level, smooth and free of traffic, and the central benches give a place to rest every few metres. The harder part is reaching it. Most hotels sit above or below the street on steep lanes with steps, so ask for a room with a short, gentle approach if anyone in your group walks slowly, and use a taxi to the nearest end of the street after dark.
list: Walk on the left half of the street and leave the centre benches for people who want to sit.
Ask before photographing monks, children or shopkeepers. Most will say yes; some will not.
Do not feed the street dogs scraps from your plate; use a bin.
Queue at the ATMs and the momo counters. Gangtok queues are orderly.
Dress as you like, but cover up a little more if you are heading on to a monastery the same day.
Do not argue loudly with shopkeepers over prices; most MG Marg shops have fixed prices.
Keep children close in the evening crowd, especially during festivals and the December food festival.

sections.heading: Making the most of an evening on MG Marg
paras: The street is at its best from about 5 to 9 pm, when the lamps come on and families from Gangtok come out to walk. In December, the Gangtok Food and Culture Festival is held on MG Marg, with stalls from across the state. On public holidays and festival days the street fills early, so come before 5 pm if you want a bench.

At the southern end, the lanes drop down to Lal Bazaar, the town's main market, built in 1956 and named after John S. Lall, the first Dewan of Sikkim under the Chogyal. It now sits in the multi-storey Kanchendzonga Shopping Complex, with a vegetable floor and a Sunday haat when village sellers come to town. Near MG Marg you will also find a statue group showing Khye Bumsa, the Bhutia ancestor, with the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and his wife Nyokong Ngal. Sikkimese tradition holds that Khye Bumsa and Thekong Tek swore a pact of blood brotherhood at Kabi Lungchok, which is remembered at the Pang Lhabsol festival.
Most shops close by 8–9 pm. Restaurants stay open a little later, but Gangtok is an early town. Plan to be back at your hotel by about 10 pm, especially in winter.

sections.heading: Getting there and practical notes
paras: Since no vehicles enter the street, your taxi will drop you at one of its ends. From the Deorali stand on NH10, a local shared taxi to the MG Marg area costs ₹20–40 a seat, indicative 2026. Children's Park, beside MG Marg, has a stand for short runs to other parts of town, and the SNT bus stand on Paljor Stadium Road is a 6–7 minute walk away.

MG Marg and the lanes around it have ATMs, pharmacies, mobile shops and travel desks. Many hotels in our budget and mid-range lists sit within 10 minutes' walk, which saves taxi money every evening. Wheelchair users will find the street itself level and smooth, but most approaches from the side lanes involve steps or steep ramps; check the route with your hotel before you book.

faqs.q: Is smoking allowed on MG Marg Gangtok
faqs.a: No. Smoking is banned on MG Marg and in public places across Gangtok, and fines have been ₹200, the amount allowed under India's national tobacco law and quoted by Gangtok's municipal corporation. Police and municipal staff patrol the street in the evening. If you smoke, ask your hotel where you may do so and carry a pocket ashtray. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the fine for littering on MG Marg
faqs.a: Gangtok Municipal Corporation has listed littering fines from ₹200 to ₹5,000, with ₹5,000 for using banned plastic or throwing garbage into drains. In practice a first slip often brings a warning, but do not count on it. Use the bins, or carry your rubbish back to the hotel. Amounts change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are vehicles allowed on MG Marg
faqs.a: No. MG Marg is a pedestrian-only street of about 1 km, and cars, taxis, two-wheelers and cycles are not allowed on it. Taxis drop you at either end. If someone in your group has limited mobility, ask your driver to use the end with the fewest steps, and plan the walk in short stretches with rests on the central benches.

faqs.q: Can I carry plastic bags in Gangtok
faqs.a: Avoid them. Shops in Gangtok are not supposed to hand out banned plastic, Sikkim has banned polystyrene products statewide, and municipal fines for banned plastic have been up to ₹5,000. Carry a cloth bag for shopping and a refillable water bottle. Bags you arrive with in your luggage are not a problem, but do not leave them anywhere.

faqs.q: What time is MG Marg busiest
faqs.a: From about 5 to 9 pm, when the lamps come on and Gangtok families come out to walk. It is also busy on weekend afternoons and during the December food festival. For quiet photographs, go between 7 and 9 am, when shops are still shuttered and the benches are empty. Most shops close by 8–9 pm.

faqs.q: Is MG Marg safe at night
faqs.a: Yes, by Indian standards it is one of the safest town centres in the hills, with police on patrol in the evening. The usual care applies in crowds: keep phones and wallets in front pockets and children close. The lanes off the street are steep and poorly lit in places, so carry a phone torch when walking back to your hotel.

faqs.q: What is there to do on MG Marg
faqs.a: Walk, sit on the benches, eat and shop. The street has cafes, bakeries, momo shops, bookshops, handicraft stores and travel desks for booking Tsomgo and Nathu La trips. Lal Bazaar, the main market, is a short walk down the lanes at the southern end. In December, the Gangtok Food and Culture Festival fills the street with food stalls.

faqs.q: Is spitting paan or gutka fined in Gangtok
faqs.a: Yes. Spitting in public places has been fined ₹200 in Gangtok, and MG Marg is marked as a spit-free zone. This is the rule visitors from the plains most often break without thinking, so leave paan and gutka at home or at least off the street. Shopkeepers are quick to point it out, and staff on patrol can fine you.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on MG Marg
faqs.a: Not on the street itself. Drinking in public places is not allowed, and police on patrol will stop it. Licensed bars and restaurants on and around MG Marg serve alcohol indoors, and most close by about 10 pm. Do not carry open bottles or cans on the street, and do not leave empties on the benches, since that also counts as littering.
